title: What I'd tell myself in year one of Trust & Safety
point: Five lessons from more than ten years in the field: treat safety as a systems problem built into the product, don't treat a ban as a closed case, measure what users experience rather than how busy the team was, let automation earn its scope, and give every risk one named owner.

title: Financial sextortion moves in hours, so start with what the teen sees
point: Financial sextortion can go from first contact to a payment demand inside a day, too fast for grooming detection built for weeks. Start with defaults that limit who can message a teen and notices about strangers, then a fast, shame-free response with an on-call emergency referral and a CyberTipline report.

title: What I'm reading: an open policy model, Xbox's adult checks, Discord in Brazil and KOSA
point: An open-weights model that scores a message against your written policy in milliseconds (Musubi's PolicyLM-1.7B, which the Workbench's classifier eval can now run), Xbox marking some long-time accounts as adults from their account activity, a Brazilian interim order for Discord to add age verification and parental supervision, and KOSA now needing a recorded Senate vote.

title: If a regulator asked for your pre-launch risk record tomorrow
point: Ofcom's investigation into whether Meta risk-assessed Instagram Instants before launch is a test any service with UK users could face. Do the assessment at design review with a named sign-off, decide how disappearing content gets reported, and file a dated record you could hand over within a day.

title: What I'm reading: Ofcom and Instagram Instants, Ofcom's data demands in court, and Roblox in Kansas
point: Ofcom is investigating whether Meta risk-assessed Instagram Instants before launch, and Meta, TikTok and X are challenging Ofcom's demands for moderation data in court. Kansas settled with Roblox for more than $10 million plus age checks and age-grouped chat, and OpenAI's own tests show its new EU text watermark weakens when 10% of the words are swapped.

title: Launch week is the hardest test a safety program gets
point: Most of what goes wrong in launch week is decided before day one. Pre-approve friction for new and unverified accounts, triage by severity, watch the rate of abuse rather than raw counts, and agree with product how much friction you'll accept, then review it after week one.

title: Since 2024, the job is proving it works
point: Since 2024 the question has moved from whether you have a policy to whether you can show it works: UK risk assessments that must be redone before significant changes, age assurance as the foundation, 48-hour removal of intimate images under the US TAKE IT DOWN Act, and free open-source tooling. Those duties land on different teams, so the leadership team should name one owner for the whole picture.

title: Saturday reading: child safety gaps in games, Ofcom in court and California's new laws
point: Australia's eSafety found Fortnite and Minecraft still mostly rely on self-declared age. Age assurance is the foundation, because every other safeguard assumes you know who's a kid.

title: Watch the rate, not the volume
point: In live sports chat, volume swings hard while the rate of abusive content tends to hold steady. Alert on rate jumps to spot raids, and slow down new accounts instead of locking the room.

title: Run the abuse pre-mortem at design review
point: At design review, changing a default is a quick edit. After launch it means taking something away. T&S earns the invite by being selective and fast, and accepted risks get an owner and a date.

title: Harassed players look like your best-retained users
point: Raw retention data hides the cost of toxicity because harassed players are the most engaged. A matched cohort shows it, and safety exposure belongs on the retention dashboard.

title: A proper introduction
point: Who Steven is and what to expect: T&S news with a practitioner's context, focused on child safety, age assurance, gaming and platform compliance, plus free tools.

title: Why early grooming detection matters
point: Tools that help platforms spot grooming early protect kids and the communities around them.

title: Launches get a security review. Almost none get an abuse review.
point: Introducing the free abuse pre-mortem: 12 questions, rated risks, safeguards with owners in priority order, likely laws, and a launch plan for Jira, Linear or GitHub.

title: Grooming is a pattern, not a message
point: Responses build as signals stack on adult-to-minor contact, with thresholds tested on past cases, a queue worked by risk, privacy limits agreed up front, and four numbers that show it works.

title: Nudify apps: harm no single platform sees in full
point: The image is made on one service, the tool promoted on another and the harm lands on a third. That's why cross-platform signal sharing through Lantern matters.

title: Age assurance: what should each check unlock?
point: The method matters less than what each level of assurance lets a user do. Errors aren't equal, accounts change hands, and someone has to own the thresholds.

title: The era of voluntary child safety is ending
point: India's push for age checks, Florida's case against OpenAI, Copilot data labeling, TikTok's Alabama settlement and Meta's New Mexico verdict. The question has moved from "do you have a policy?" to "can you prove it works?"

title: Games are where kids socialize now, and regulators know it
point: Grooming builds over weeks and usually moves off-platform. Protections that work act earlier and limit who can reach a child. Measure prevented contact, not just removals.

title: A banned account is not a closed case
point: Online enticement is a pattern of contact, not a file, and is now mandatory to report. The hard call is the account: ban visibly, or restrict quietly while the network is mapped.

title: Appeal overturns: the early warning for automation
point: Overturned appeals show drift weeks before anything else. Automation expands only where its overturn rate matches human review, and changes roll back when the rate moves.

title: Activity is easy to measure. Impact is harder.
point: A 40% jump in removals could mean better detection, more harm or over-enforcement. Report outcome metrics next to operational ones, and tell leadership when they disagree.

title: Automation rate isn't a measure of maturity
point: Automate as much as the evidence supports. Where a wrong decision can't be reversed or someone's safety is at risk, automation prepares the case and a person closes it.

title: You can't moderate your way out of a systems problem
point: Treating Trust & Safety mainly as an operations function is a mistake. Reputation, history, age and behavior signals belong in one risk model, automation needs clear limits, and safety belongs in the product architecture from the start.
